Raised by the Swahili translator: mobile money is how East Africa pays, and the section reached it only through the QR row's `text_alt` (`Kulipa kwa M-Pesa?`), which is exactly where it was buried. Scoped on a rule the packs' own QR rows settle rather than on the geography of the request: where a wallet is paid by *scanning*, `pay-by-qr-code` already reaches it, and those packs say so themselves -- id and jv print `QRIS` in `text`, hi/kn/ml carry UPI in `text_alt` or `literal`, ur names Raast, JazzCash and Easypaisa, bn names bKash and Nagad. What is different in KE, TZ, UG, CD and ET is that the payment is a till or paybill number keyed on the phone rather than a scan, so no existing row gets there. UPI is a bank-to-bank rail initiated by a QR and is a different animal; if anyone wants a row for it, it is its own concept. fr (SN, CI) and ha (NE) were weighed and refused: mobile money is dominant in 2 of French's 6 regions and 1 of Hausa's 2, and unlike `numbers-money.franc` -- which a Senegal card has to print because the currency is what the traveller counts -- a fourth payment method is a row taken from something else on a card that will be read in France or in Kano. Nigeria's question is "can I transfer?", a bank transfer to an account number, which is a third thing again. Below `pay-by-card` because a card works on arrival and a wallet needs a local SIM; above `pay-cash` so that no trim which keeps cash drops the rail the scope's four countries actually run on.

Italy's `coperto` is a fixed per-person charge that is neither a service charge nor a tip, so `etiquette.is-service-included` does not find it: the honest answer to that question in Italy is usually no, and the bill still carries a line the traveller did not order. Asked before sitting down rather than after eating, which is also why it is not in `etiquette` -- that section is about conduct after the fact. Its own cluster and not a rung of `etiquette.service-charge`, for the reason the dengue row gives against clustering with malaria: they are different money, so a card that already carries one gains a full row's worth from the other. Scoped to the four packs whose own bills carry the line -- coperto, couvert, kouver and kuver. es is deliberately out: a Spanish bill charges the bread as an item you can decline, not as a fixed per-person cover. Japan's otoshi-dai is the same shape and is the widening a reviewer should weigh first; it is recorded in the ja row's `literal` rather than asserted here. Importance just above `is-tax-included`, because tax is at least implied by a posted price and this charge is not posted anywhere.
